recent_facts.fact: The National reported that the East-West pipeline had restarted and was pumping at a low rate. Its only sources were unnamed Reuters sources and satellite-data analysis. The article cited no statement from Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy, the government or Aramco.

The Reuters story, headlined 'Saudi Arabia restarts East-West oil pipeline, to resume exports from Yanbu, sources say', credits the restart to unnamed sources. Aramco was trying to bring flow back to 4 million bpd, below the system's full capacity of 7 million bpd.

The Saudi-owned Asharq Al-Awsat also carried the restart under the headline 'Sources: Saudi Arabia Restarts East-West Oil Pipeline', so the report is again attributed to sources and not to an official announcement.
Sources said reaching about 40% of capacity would take a couple of days and a full restart would take 6 to 8 weeks. Another source put the full restart at up to six weeks.

Pumping has resumed at reduced rates, and tanker loadings at Yanbu appear to have restarted this week, but regular exports have not recovered. Two tankers due to load on September 23 had not loaded, and six more were scheduled for September 24–27.

Sources said volumes on the East-West pipeline were building but tanker loading at Yanbu was delayed. Reuters reported that Aramco told European refiners it first needed to build a 'critical mass' of crude at Yanbu.
Industrial Info Resources cited satellite imagery showing vessels loading crude at Yanbu after the pipeline attack.

The Ministry of Energy's statement on SPA was headlined 'East–West Pipeline Shut Down as a Precaution Following Multiple Attacks'. The ministry also posted it on X and said emergency teams were deployed to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.

Saudi Arabia shut the East-West crude pipeline after several drone attacks launched from Iraq hit it in the Riyadh and Medina regions. Satellite imagery and industry sources reported that 3 of its 11 pumping stations were damaged.

There is a precedent from April 2026. On April 9 the Ministry of Energy said attacks had cut about 700,000 bpd of East-West pipeline capacity, and around April 12 it announced on SPA that full pumping capacity of about 7 million bpd had been restored.

Argaam carried the April Ministry of Energy statement that the energy facilities and the East-West line had recovered and regained their operating capacity. The ministry has made such a restoration announcement at least once before.

The 1,200 km pipeline links the eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and has been rerouting about 4 million bpd around the Strait of Hormuz. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said Riyadh would hold off retaliating to give Iraq's government time to stop attacks from its territory.
The US Energy Secretary said the Saudi East-West pipeline would be back in operation within days. This came from a third party (not the Saudi government) and was about the future.

The questions resolve Yes only if official Saudi government information says the pipeline is operating now; partial capacity counts. The Saudi-owned Asharq Al-Awsat also carried the restart under the headline 'Sources: Saudi Arabia Restarts East-West Oil Pipeline', so the report is again attributed to sources and not to an official announcement.
Sources said reaching about 40% of capacity would take a couple of days and a full restart would take 6 to 8 weeks. Another source put the full restart at up to six weeks.

Sources said volumes on the East-West pipeline were building but tanker loading at Yanbu was delayed. Reuters reported that Aramco told European refiners it first needed to build a 'critical mass' of crude at Yanbu.

market.rules:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if Donald Trump signs an executive order, proclamation, or presidential memorandum that adopts a new official name for artificial intelligence, or directs a federal agency or the federal government to adopt one, by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

A qualifying action must replace or supersede "artificial intelligence" as the federal government's designation for the technology itself. Any replacement name qualifies, including "Superior Intelligence", "Extreme Intelligence", "Supreme Intelligence", or "Genius Intelligence"; the name chosen has no bearing on resolution. An order that directs an agency to adopt or implement such a name within a stated period qualifies.

Statements, speeches, interviews, press conferences, and social media posts, including polls posted to social media, do not count. Renaming a federal office, agency, program, task force, commission, or military service, such as an "AI Force", does not count unless the same action also renames the technology itself. Renaming a specific product, model, or private-sector system does not count. Incidental use of an alternative term in the text of an order, without a directive adopting it as the official designation, does not count.

The signing or issuance of a qualifying order within this market's timeframe will qualify for a "Yes" resolution, regardless of when the order takes effect, and regardless of whether it is subsequently stayed, enjoined, revoked, or superseded.

The primary resolution source will be official information from the government of the United States, including the text of presidential actions published at whitehouse.gov and in the Federal Register; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

recent_facts.fact: The newest item on the White House presidential actions page is the Gold Star Mother's and Family's Day proclamation of Sept 25, 2026. None of the actions listed from Sept 16–25 (including H-1B, angling, hunting and procurement orders) mentions artificial intelligence, super intelligence or renaming AI.

In his Sept 22, 2026 UN General Assembly speech, Trump said the federal government would rename AI 'super intelligence.' He said that 'from this point forward, all of United States documents' would use 'super' instead of 'artificial.'

Breaking Defense reported that Trump gave the directive verbally at the UN, citing no signed executive order or formal memo, and said 'As of yet, there is no official announcement from the White House on how this is to be implemented.'

Michael Drager, a Deputy Assistant Secretary in the State Department's international organizations bureau, sent staff an email titled 'Change in Nomenclature AI to SI.' Citing 'the president's remarks at the GA today,' it told them to replace 'Artificial Intelligence' with 'Super Intelligence' in all remarks, positions and press elements. It was an agency email, not a presidential document.

US representatives had already started using 'SI' at UN Security Council meetings. Euronews said it was unclear whether the directive applied beyond the State Department's international organizations bureau.

This explainer said no executive order or Federal Register filing had yet made the 'Super Intelligence' switch binding. It said existing federal orders and the AI Action Plan still use 'Artificial Intelligence.'

According to Gizmodo's headline, the White House said Trump got China's Xi Jinping to agree to call AI 'super intelligence.' Trump posted that Xi 'seemed to like' the idea.

A diplomatic meeting occurs when representatives of both listed countries who are acting in an official capacity and are authorized to engage in diplomacy on behalf of their respective governments or governing authorities deliberately meet for the purpose of diplomacy or negotiation. A qualifying meeting need not result in any agreement, joint statement, or further engagement.

A diplomatic meeting is senior-level if each listed entity is represented by a head of state, a head of government, or a vice president; a foreign minister; a minister of cabinet rank; the secretary or head of a national security council; the presiding officer of a national legislature; a special envoy; or another individual designated by the head of state or head of government to conduct diplomatic negotiations on their behalf. Individuals authorized only for technical, implementation, monitoring, staff-level, preparatory, or working-group-level talks will not be considered designated to conduct diplomatic negotiations on behalf of the head of state or head of government. In each case, a qualifying representative must participate in the meeting.

A direct meeting refers to a diplomatic meeting where the representatives of both countries directly interact with each other in person. Meetings conducted through translators qualify, provided direct, face-to-face communication occurs. An indirect meeting refers to a meeting conducted indirectly through designated mediators or facilitators. A qualifying indirect meeting must meet both of the following criteria (i) the designated intermediaries act with the knowledge and authorization of both entities; (ii) representatives of both entities are physically present in the same facility, venue, or city as part of a single organized round of talks convened for the purpose of diplomatic engagement, with the intermediary conveying communications between the representatives or delegations on the same day. “The same day” means the same calendar day local time at the meeting location.

Sessions, proceedings, or convenings of standing international organizations, treaty bodies, or recurring multilateral summits or conferences (e.g., the United Nations General Assembly, G7, and G20 summits) do not qualify, unless a qualifying and deliberate diplomatic meeting between representatives of the listed countries is separately held alongside such a convening.

The following do not qualify as either a direct or indirect diplomatic meeting: chance encounters; standalone exchanges limited to greetings, courtesies, or photo opportunities; meetings conducted remotely, by telephone, or by any other means where the relevant representatives are not physically present at the same facility, venue, or city on the same day; discussions involving persons not authorized to engage in diplomacy or negotiation on behalf of their respective governments.

Renaming a federal office, agency, program, task force, commission, or military service, such as an "AI Force", does not count unless the same action also renames the technology itself. Incidental use of an alternative term in the text of an order, without a directive adopting it as the official designation, does not count.

The signing or issuance of a qualifying order within this market's timeframe will qualify for a "Yes" resolution, regardless of when the order takes effect, and regardless of whether it is subsequently stayed, enjoined, revoked, or superseded.

The primary resolution source will be official information from the government of the United States, including the text of presidential actions published at whitehouse.gov and in the Federal Register; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

The Reuters story, headlined 'Saudi Arabia restarts East-West oil pipeline, to resume exports from Yanbu, sources say', credits the restart to unnamed sources. Aramco was trying to bring flow back to 4 million bpd, below the system's full capacity of 7 million bpd.

The Saudi-owned Asharq Al-Awsat also carried the restart under the headline 'Sources: Saudi Arabia Restarts East-West Oil Pipeline', so the report is again attributed to sources and not to an official announcement.

Pumping has resumed at reduced rates, and tanker loadings at Yanbu appear to have restarted this week, but regular exports have not recovered. Two tankers due to load on September 23 had not loaded, and six more were scheduled for September 24–27.

Sources said volumes on the East-West pipeline were building but tanker loading at Yanbu was delayed. Reuters reported that Aramco told European refiners it first needed to build a 'critical mass' of crude at Yanbu.
Industrial Info Resources cited satellite imagery showing vessels loading crude at Yanbu after the pipeline attack.

The Ministry of Energy's statement on SPA was headlined 'East–West Pipeline Shut Down as a Precaution Following Multiple Attacks'. The ministry also posted it on X and said emergency teams were deployed to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.

Saudi Arabia shut the East-West crude pipeline after several drone attacks launched from Iraq hit it in the Riyadh and Medina regions. Satellite imagery and industry sources reported that 3 of its 11 pumping stations were damaged.

Argaam carried the April Ministry of Energy statement that the energy facilities and the East-West line had recovered and regained their operating capacity. The ministry has made such a restoration announcement at least once before.

The 1,200 km pipeline links the eastern oil fields to the Red Sea port of Yanbu and has been rerouting about 4 million bpd around the Strait of Hormuz. The Saudi Foreign Ministry said Riyadh would hold off retaliating to give Iraq's government time to stop attacks from its territory.

On September 22, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, with President Trump saying another meeting is scheduled in the near future.(see: https://www.israelhayom.com/2026/09/22/witkoff-kushner-attended-us-iran-meeting-another-expected-soon). 

This market will resolve to “Yes” if there is a direct or indirect senior-level diplomatic meeting between the United States and Iran by the listed date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A diplomatic meeting occurs when representatives of both listed countries who are acting in an official capacity and are authorized to engage in diplomacy on behalf of their respective governments or governing authorities deliberately meet for the purpose of diplomacy or negotiation. A qualifying meeting need not result in any agreement, joint statement, or further engagement.

A diplomatic meeting is senior-level if each listed entity is represented by a head of state, a head of government, or a vice president; a foreign minister; a minister of cabinet rank; the secretary or head of a national security council; the presiding officer of a national legislature; a special envoy; or another individual designated by the head of state or head of government to conduct diplomatic negotiations on their behalf. Individuals authorized only for technical, implementation, monitoring, staff-level, preparatory, or working-group-level talks will not be considered designated to conduct diplomatic negotiations on behalf of the head of state or head of government. This definition includes, but is not limited to, all of the following individuals: for the United States, Donald Trump, JD Vance, Marco Rubio, Scott Bessent, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner; and for Iran, Mojtaba Khamenei, Masoud Pezeshkian, Abbas Araghchi and Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. In each case, a qualifying representative must participate in the meeting.

A direct meeting refers to a diplomatic meeting where the representatives of both countries directly interact with each other in person. Meetings conducted through translators qualify, provided direct, face-to-face communication occurs. An indirect meeting refers to a meeting conducted indirectly through designated mediators or facilitators. A qualifying indirect meeting must meet both of the following criteria (i) the designated intermediaries act with the knowledge and authorization of both entities; (ii) representatives of both entities are physically present in the same facility, venue, or city as part of a single organized round of talks convened for the purpose of diplomatic engagement, with the intermediary conveying communications between the representatives or delegations on the same day. “The same day” means the same calendar day local time at the meeting location.

Sessions, proceedings, or convenings of standing international organizations, treaty bodies, or recurring multilateral summits or conferences (e.g., the United Nations General Assembly, G7, and G20 summits) do not qualify, unless a qualifying and deliberate diplomatic meeting between representatives of the listed countries is separately held alongside such a convening.

The following do not qualify as either a direct or indirect diplomatic meeting: chance encounters; standalone exchanges limited to greetings, courtesies, or photo opportunities; meetings conducted remotely, by telephone, or by any other means where the relevant representatives are not physically present at the same facility, venue, or city on the same day; discussions involving persons not authorized to engage in diplomacy or negotiation on behalf of their respective governments.

The resolution sources for this market will be official information from the governments of the United States and Iran and a consensus of credible reporting.
